(uncountable) The property or characteristic of being ostentatious.

English osteo-
English arthritis

From osteo- + arthritis.

s.d: chronic breakdown of cartilage in the joints; the most common form of arthritis occurring usually after middle age
(uncountable) A form of arthritis, affecting mainly older people, caused by chronic degeneration of the cartilage and synovial membrane of the joints, leading to pain and stiffness.
a cell from which bone develops
benign tumor of bone and fibrous tissue; occurs in the vertebrae or femur or tibia or arm bones (especially in young adults)
an uncommon osteoid tissue-forming primary neoplasm of the bone
benign tumor containing both bone and cartilage; usually occurs near the end of a long bone
A benign tumor consisting of bone or cartilage
treatment of a skeletal deformity by intentionally fracturing a bone
(uncountable) The surgical fracture of a bone in order to correct a deformity
cell that functions in the breakdown and resorption of bone tissue
A large multinuclear cell associated with the resorption of bone.
x: Inhibition of osteoclast activation and differentiation is an effective strategy for blocking bone resorption.

s.d: An instrument for performing osteoclasis.

(uncountable) Any abnormal or defective development of a bone
autosomal dominant disorder of connective tissue characterized by brittle bones that fracture easily
(uncountable) A hereditary disease characterized by brittle bones that easily fracture.
malignant bone tumor; most common in children and young adults where it tends to affect the femur
an anatomist who is skilled in osteology
an osteologist.
an anatomist who is skilled in osteology
A scientist or physician whose speciality is osteology.
the branch of anatomy that studies the bones of the vertebrate skeleton
(uncountable) The scientific study of the morphology and pathology of bones.
(uncountable) The bone structure of a particular individual, or species.
lysis of bone caused by disease or infection or inadequate blood supply
(uncountable) The resorption or dissolution of bone tissue.
a slow growing benign tumor of consisting of bone tissue; usually on the skull or mandible
A benign bony tumour that typically grows on the skull.

s.d: abnormal softening of bones caused by deficiencies of phosphorus or calcium or vitamin D
(uncountable) A softening of adult bones due to inadequate mineralization; the adult equivalent of rickets.

a therapist who manipulates the skeleton and muscles

A non-physician healthcare practitioner who practices osteopathy by manipulating the skeleton and muscles. Not to be confused with Doctors of Osteopathic Medicine (D.O.) (also known as osteopathic physicians) who are full physicians like Doctors of Medicine (M.D.).
a therapist who manipulates the skeleton and muscles
An osteopath.
therapy based on the assumption that restoring health is best accomplished by manipulating the skeleton and muscles
(uncountable) The branch of therapy based on manipulation of bones and muscles.
(rare, uncountable) Any disease of the bones.

s.d: an inherited disorder characterized by an increase in bone density; in severe forms the bone marrow cavity may be obliterated
(uncountable) A rare hereditary disorder characterized by hard, dense bones.

osteophyte.e: From French ostéophyte. Surface reading of osteo- (“bone”) + -phyte (“growth”).

s.d: small abnormal bony outgrowth
A small, abnormal growth of bone (exostosis, bone spur) that forms along joint margins.

osteoporosis.e: From Ancient Greek ὀστέον (ostéon, “bone”) + Ancient Greek πώρωσις (pṓrōsis, “petrification, callousness”), from Ancient Greek πῶρος (pôros, “tuff, a porous type of rock”). By surface analysis, osteo- + pore + -osis.

s.d: abnormal loss of bony tissue resulting in fragile porous bones attributable to a lack of calcium; most common in postmenopausal women
(uncountable) A disease, occurring especially in women following menopause, in which the bones become extremely porous and are subject to fracture.

osteosarcoma.e:

Ancient Greek ὀστέον (ostéon)der.
English osteo-
English sarcoma
English osteosarcoma
From osteo- + sarcoma.

s.d: malignant bone tumor; most common in children and young adults where it tends to affect the femur
A type of cancer of the bone.
x: Even small osteosarcomas can be unimaginably painful.

(uncountable) An increase in bone density
an inherited skeletal disorder beginning before birth; cartilage is converted to bone resulting in dwarfism
extinct jawless fish of the Devonian with armored head
Any extinct fish of the class Osteostraci

s.d: surgical sectioning of bone
The surgical procedure of cutting a bone. This is often performed to either lengthen, shorten, or straighten a bone.
the lowest of the minor Holy Orders in the unreformed Western Church but now suppressed by the Roman Catholic Church
(historical) An ostiary; a doorman; a porter.
A student office held by a prefect with the duties of keeping order, collecting the vulguses, and ensuring the other students attend class.

ostiary.e: Borrowed from Latin ostiārius, from ostium (“door, entrance”). See usher, which may be a doublet.

s.d: the lowest of the minor Holy Orders in the unreformed Western Church but now suppressed by the Roman Catholic Church
someone who guards an entrance
(archaic) The mouth of a river; an estuary.
x: the river of Nilus hath seven ostiaries, that is, by seven channels disburdened itself into the sea

s.d: One who keeps the door, especially the door of a church; a porter.
x: So arrayed I stepped at last from my door and was saluted as before by my monstrous ostiaries.

ostinato.e: From Italian ostinato (“stubborn”). Doublet of obstinate.

s.d: a musical phrase repeated over and over during a composition
A piece of melody, a chord progression, or a bass figure that is repeated over and over as a musical accompaniment.
x: The piece moves in alluring spans of swirling figures, jagged lines and pointillistic outbursts, often prodded forward by ostinatos in the perky piano.

s.d: a small pore especially one in the reproductive bodies of certain algae and fungi through which spores pass
A small hole or opening through which certain fungi release their mature spores.
A similar hole or opening in plants, such as the opening of the involuted fig inflorescence through which fig wasps enter to pollinate and breed.

ostler.e: Phonetic spelling of hostler, from late 14th century.

s.d: someone employed in a stable to take care of the horses
A person employed at an inn, hostelry, or stable to look after horses; a groom.
x: Followed by the sun, I left the grounds of the mansion and entered the deserted park, an ostler leading a large and passive work-horse out to the day's labour.

ostomy.e: Back-formation from colostomy, ileostomy, gastrostomy, and similar terms.

s.d: surgical procedure that creates an artificial opening for the elimination of bodily wastes
A surgical procedure to provide an exit point for the waste of an organism.
An exit point created by such surgical procedure.

ostracism.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ὀστρακισμός (ostrakismós, “banishment by means of voting with pot shards”), from ὀστρακίζω (ostrakízō, “ostracize”) + -ισμός (-ismós, “-ism”), from ὄστρακον (óstrakon, “clay pot”).

s.d: the state of being banished or ostracized (excluded from society by general consent)
x: the association should get rid of its elderly members — not by euthanasia, of course, but by Coventry

s.d: the act of excluding someone from society by general consent
(historical, uncountable) In ancient Athens (and some other cities), the temporary banishment by popular vote of a citizen considered dangerous to the state.
x: Witnesse the Ostracisme amongst the Athenians, and the Petalisme among the Siracusans.

s.d: (figuratively, uncountable) Banishment by some general consent.
(uncountable) Temporary exclusion from a community or society.

ostracize.e: From Ancient Greek ὀστρακίζω (ostrakízō, “to banish from a city by ostracism”), from ὄστρᾰκον (óstrăkon, “earthenware vessel; fragment of such a vessel, potsherd”) (from the fact that when voting was held to decide whether to banish people, their names were inscribed on potsherds) + -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō, suffix forming verbs)). The English word is cognate with French ostraciser.

s.d: expel from a community or group
avoid speaking to or dealing with
x: Ever since I spoke up, my colleagues ostracize me

s.d: (US, historical) To ban a person from a city for five or ten years through the procedure of ostracism.
x: Republics have been accused of being ungrateful. Aristides was ostracised for being called the Just, and Themistocles banished, after saving his country from desolation.

[T]he person who was ostracised was obliged to leave Athens within ten days after the sentence, and unless a vote of the people recalled him before the expiration of that time, to stay in exile for ten years.

s.d: (US) To exclude a person from a community or from society by not communicating with them or by refusing to acknowledge their presence; to refuse to associate with or talk to; to shun.
x: You then moſt Noble Equivocations and Alluſions, whom Rhetorick would Oſtraciſe, ſeek Revenge for your Baniſhment; [...]

The inflexible advocate[s] of the people's rights, were either expelled the Senate Chamber, ostracised, or immolated on the reeking altars of patriotism, by the encrimsoned sword of slaughtering persecution.

ostracod.e: From Ancient Greek ὀστρακώδης (ostrakṓdēs, “covered with shell”), from ὄστρακον (óstrakon, “clay pot; shell”); compare translingual Ostracoda.

s.d: tiny marine and freshwater crustaceans with a shrimp-like body enclosed in a bivalve shell
Any of many small crustaceans, of the class Ostracoda, that resemble a shrimp enclosed in a bivalve shell.
x: Considering all the ecological data, there seems to be an evolution in the associations of ostracods throughout time.
This study has also shown that the fifth limb is most probably of thoracic origin and hence ostracods have only one pair of maxillae.

ostracoderm.e: From New Latin ostracum, from Ancient Greek ὄστρακον (óstrakon, “pottery fragment; shell”) + δέρμα (dérma, “skin”).

s.d: extinct fish-like jawless vertebrate having a heavily armored body; of the Paleozoic
Any of the armored jawless fishes of the Paleozoic.

ostrich.e: From Middle English ostrich, ostriche, ostryche, ostrige, borrowed from Anglo-Norman ostrige and Old French ostruce, from Vulgar Latin *austruthio, from Latin avis (“bird”) + strūthiō (“ostrich”), from Ancient Greek στρουθίων (strouthíōn), or shortened from strūthiocamēlus, from Ancient Greek στρουθοκᾰ́μηλος (strouthokắmēlos), from στρουθός (strouthós, “sparrow”) + κάμηλος (kámēlos, “camel”). Compare Spanish avestruz and Portuguese avestruz.

s.d: a person who refuses to face reality or recognize the truth (a reference to the popular notion that the ostrich hides from danger by burying its head in the sand)
fast-running African flightless bird with two-toed feet; largest living bird
A large flightless bird of the order Struthioniformes.
A large flightless bird of the order Struthioniformes.: The most widespread species of that order, known as the common ostrich (Struthio camelus).
x: Could a Taff'ta ſcarf, a long Eſtridge vvhing, / A ſtiffe Iron Doublet, and a Brazeel Pole / Tempt thee from Cambrick ſheets, fine active Thighs, / From Caudles vvhere the precious Amber ſvvims?
The San Juan market is Mexico City's most famous deli of exotic meats, where an adventurous shopper can hunt down hard-to-find critters such as ostrich, wild boar and crocodile.

s.d: (obsolete) The rhea.
x: The Lengua Indians of the Gran Chaco love to hunt the ostrich

s.d: (figuratively) One who buries their head in the sand instead of acknowledging problems.
The hypothetical completion of a hole five strokes under par (a quintuple birdie, quadruple eagle, triple albatross, or double condor).
tall fern of northern temperate regions having graceful arched fronds and sporophylls resembling ostrich plumes

Any member of the species Matteuccia struthiopteris, a crown-forming, colony-forming fern occurring in temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere in eastern and northern Europe, northern Asia and northern North America.
perennial aromatic herb of eastern North America having variously colored tubular flowers in dense showy heads
(uncountable) An American aromatic herb (Monarda didyma) with bright red labiate flowers; also called bee balm or bergamot.
